ledeLeadHtml: Japan warehousing and logistics grows in yen, not in tonnes — Not Rated at sector level; base cases for the Big 3 cluster at +17% to +19%
ledeHtml:
This report initiates J-Core coverage of the Japan warehousing and logistics sector — TSE 33-sector code 5200, 29 companies in the programme universe after two scope exclusions — and answers one question first: how much does the industry grow from here? The sourced answer is narrower than the headlines suggest. On the broadest citable definition, Yano Research Institute puts the 15-sector logistics market at ¥24.794tn in FY2024, up 5.7% year on year [reported estimate], and forecasts ¥25.360tn in FY2025 (+2.3%) and ¥26.361tn in FY2026 (+3.9%) [Yano forecasts]. The narrow warehousing industry on its own was ¥2.6tn in FY2021, the latest clean total published by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT). Physical warehouse volumes, on MLIT's monthly series, are growing at roughly 0% to 2% a year: storage balances rose 2.1% to 2.3% year on year in 2025 while inbound volumes moved between −2% and +4% by month. The growth is therefore value-led, not volume-led — freight, storage and handling rate revisions after the April 2024 truck-driver overtime cap, a rising 3PL outsourcing share, and cold-chain price and mix. J-Core's synthesis, labelled as our view throughout, is total logistics growth of about +2% to +4% a year in yen, 3PL growth of about +4% to +5.5% a year on third-party definitions that differ and are not averaged, and physical warehouse volume growth of about 0% to +2% a year.

The second leg of sector returns is the balance sheet, not the income statement. The Big 3 — Mitsubishi Logistics (9301), MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS (9302) and Sumitomo Warehouse (9303) — disclosed combined rental real-estate unrealised gains of ¥488,547mn in their FY3/2026 filings (J-Core calculation from the three reported figures: ¥298,359mn, ¥102,140mn and ¥88,048mn), and real-estate segment margins of roughly 33% to 40% against logistics margins of roughly 5% to 8%. In the three company initiation reports published today, 24 November 2026, each of the Big 3 is rated Overweight on base cases of ¥1,450 (+16.9%), ¥3,800 (+18.8%) and ¥4,500 (+17.3%). The sector itself is Not Rated: the scenario ranges are 54 to 60 percentage points wide, because execution and asset-value surfacing — not the industry cycle — decide outcomes.

blocks.heading: 1. The central question — how much does the industry grow?
blocks.html:
Every figure in this section carries its owner and its status. [Reported] means a published statistic or actual. [Forecast] means a named forecaster's projection. [Calculated] means arithmetic on a source's own published endpoints. Where a figure could not be verified from a public source, it is marked not obtained rather than estimated.

Start with the two market-size anchors, which measure different things and must not be mixed. The narrow warehousing industry (倉庫業) — commercial warehouse operators — recorded operating revenue of ¥2.6tn in FY2021, across 6,582 operators, 98.9% of them small and medium-sized enterprises, employing about 132,000 people [reported: MLIT, Logistics in Numbers 2023, as presented by the Japan Warehousing Association to an MLIT study group on 10 December 2024]. MLIT has published no newer national total in the sources found, so ¥2.6tn is the latest clean citable figure and this report does not update it by extrapolation. The broader logistics market — Yano Research Institute's sum of operator sales across 15 sectors, including some duplication between sectors — was ¥24.794tn in FY2024, 105.7% of FY2023 [reported estimate: Yano press release No. 4142, 5 August 2026]. Yano forecasts ¥25.360tn for FY2025 (+2.3%) and ¥26.361tn for FY2026 (+3.9%) [forecast: Yano, same release]. The two-year path implies about +3.1% a year [calculated].

Two cross-checks discipline those numbers. First, forecast error: Yano's 2025 edition put FY2024 at ¥24.641tn and forecast FY2025 at only +0.5%; the 2026 edition revised FY2025 to +2.3%. A one-year revision of about 1.8 percentage points on the same year is the honest error band to carry. Second, composition: Yano attributes FY2024 growth to 3PL and to international logistics, where Red Sea detours raised ocean freight and yen weakness inflated yen values, and states explicitly that a full recovery in freight volume has yet to be achieved and that market expansion is primarily driven by increased transportation unit prices and exchange rates. The +5.7% headline for FY2024 is therefore not a domestic volume figure, and the +2% to +4% forecast range for FY2025–26 is the domestic-centred rate this report underwrites.

blocks.heading: Value-led growth: volumes, prices and the J-Core synthesis
blocks.html:
Physical volumes first. MLIT's monthly series for major operators' ordinary warehouses shows inbound volumes of 2.50m tonnes in April 2025 (+3.7% year on year), 2.34m tonnes in May (−2.4%) and 2.47m tonnes in June (+3.0%), with month-end storage balances of 5.15m to 5.17m tonnes, up 2.1% year on year [reported: MLIT Monthly Economic Report, September and October 2025 issues, as corrected on 17 October 2025]. On the major-21-company average for April to November 2025, inbound volumes rose 0.3%, outbound volumes fell 1.7% and storage balances rose 2.3% [reported, via Chuo Warehouse's FY2026/3 results briefing, 29 May 2026]. Balances rising about 2% while throughput is flat means longer dwell and buffer stock, not faster flow. Ordinary warehouse floor area under management was 70.896m m² at end-June 2025 [reported: MLIT Warehouse Statistics Quarterly, FY2025 Q1].

Prices, by contrast, are moving. Refrigerated and frozen warehouse services revenue reached ¥865.0bn in 2024, up 11.9% [calculated] on the revised 2023 figure [reported: MIC/METI Economic Structure Survey], while frozen-food production volume fell 0.5% in 2024 and consumption volume rose only 1.5% [reported: Japan Frozen Foods Association, April 2025]. The gap between +11.9% revenue and roughly flat volume is price and mix. MLIT's FY2024 Warehouse Business Management Indicators add a warning from inside the industry: the ordinary-warehouse cargo-handling divisions of the 113 responding companies averaged an operating margin of −3.3% [calculated from the published per-company revenue and operating loss]. Storage alone is not where the money is; handling and 3PL services are.

J-Core synthesis — our view, not a source forecast. Total logistics grows at about +2% to +4% a year in yen on Yano's FY2025–26 forecasts. 3PL grows faster, at about +4% to +5.5% a year: IMARC Group forecasts a Japan 3PL CAGR of 4.3% for 2025–33 (US$66.7bn in 2024 to US$102.0bn in 2033) and Expert Market Research forecasts 5.4% for 2025–34 (about US$43.1bn to about US$72.9bn) [both forecasts, owners as stated]. The two houses' 2024 levels differ by about US$24bn because their definitions differ; this report does not average them, and Yano does not publish a standalone 3PL yen figure in its free releases — that figure is not obtained. Physical warehouse volumes grow at about 0% to +2% a year on the MLIT series. Company plans sit above the industry rate by construction: Sumitomo Warehouse targets revenue of ¥280.0bn by FY3/2031, about +7.5% a year [calculated from the company's plan of 31 March 2026], and MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS' revised FY3/2027 guidance of ¥330bn revenue and ¥24.0bn operating profit already exceeds its Mid-Term Plan 2022 operating-profit target of ¥23.0bn while tracking below its ¥350bn revenue target [company guidance, 6 November 2026]. Growth above about +7% a year in any Big 3 plan is, by arithmetic, share gain plus M&A plus overseas expansion, and this report underwrites it as execution, not as industry beta.

blocks.heading: 2. Drivers — labour scarcity, price pass-through and regulation
blocks.html:
The 2024 problem is the sector's pricing mechanism, and it is quantified by the government itself. MLIT estimates that, with no countermeasures, the April 2024 cap on truck-driver overtime (960 hours a year) and revised standards would leave transport capacity about 14% short in FY2024 and about 34% short in FY2030 [reported: MLIT study group report, 2025, using NX Research Institute estimates]. The cabinet's Comprehensive Logistics Policy Outline 2026–2030 (cabinet decision, 31 March 2026) assesses that the FY2024 shortfall was broadly overcome through load-efficiency gains — truck load efficiency rose from 37.7% in FY2019 to 41.3% in FY2024 — modal shift and fewer re-deliveries, while capacity remains tight. The shortage is demographic, not cyclical: drivers aged 15 to 29 were 10.1% of the driver workforce in 2024, against 16.8% across all industries, and large-truck drivers earned ¥4.92m in 2024 against an all-industry average of ¥5.27m while working 2,484 hours against 2,052.

Price followed scarcity. On 22 March 2024 MLIT raised standard truck freight (標準的運賃) by an average of about 8%, moved the fuel surcharge base to ¥120 per litre, made a subcontracting fee of 10% of freight separately chargeable, and itemised loading, unloading and waiting charges [reported: MLIT notification, 22 March 2024]. Pass-through is visible in shippers' own costs: the JILS shipper logistics-cost ratio rose to 5.44% of sales in its 2024 survey, up 0.44pt year on year and the second-highest in 20 years [reported: JILS, summary 28 April 2025]; the 2025 survey put the ratio at 5.32%. Warehousing's own catch-up is earlier-stage: the Japan Warehousing Association notes that the ordinary-warehouse storage-fee index has been broadly flat since 2000 while construction costs have risen sharply, and there is no warehouse equivalent of the truck standard-freight benchmark. Sumitomo Warehouse's March 2026 plan review blames part of its previous plan's profit miss — revenue target ¥230bn against about ¥195bn forecast, operating profit target ¥18bn against ¥11bn — on delayed pass-through of cost increases into rates. Pass-through was not automatic before 2024–25; that is both the headroom and the risk.

Warehouses are inside the same mechanism. The cabinet-decided sectoral operating policy of 23 January 2026 projects the logistics-warehouse sector to be about 55,100 workers short in FY2028, to be filled by productivity improvement including warehouse-management systems (about 20,300), domestic workforce participation (about 16,500) and foreign workers (about 18,300) [reported]. The industry job-offer-to-applicant ratio was 2.54 in 2024, and warehouse-sector spring wage settlements rose from 1.87% in FY2019 to 5.69% in FY2024. Automation demand follows: logistics-systems equipment sales were ¥657.0bn in FY2024 (+3.8%), of which automated warehouses were ¥147.1bn (+11.4%) [reported: JILS/JIMH], and FY2025 sales of ¥690.7bn were a record. Two cautions apply: a large share of equipment growth is cleanroom (semiconductor) and overseas demand — cleanroom applications were ¥230.4bn, 35.1% of the FY2024 total [calculated share] — and the revised Logistics Efficiency Act, which imposed effort obligations on all shippers and logistics operators from 1 April 2025, makes waiting and handling time a measured, chargeable activity. Regulation is converting previously free services into revenue lines, at a compliance cost.

blocks.heading: E-commerce, 3PL outsourcing and the cold chain
blocks.html:
E-commerce is the demand driver with the longest runway, measured carefully. METI's FY2024 E-Commerce Market Survey (26 August 2025) puts the B2C EC market at ¥26.1tn in 2024, up 5.1%, with goods EC of ¥15.219tn (+3.70%) and a goods EC ratio of 9.78%, up 0.40pt [all reported]. METI's denominator is all commercial transactions in goods categories, not retail sales; on the retail-sales definition used internationally, eMarketer puts Japan's penetration at about 12.9% to 14%, the lowest of the top-five EC markets, against 15.0% for the US and 30.1% for Korea on the figures cited in the source pack. The two series must not be mixed in one chart. The structural point survives either definition: the goods EC ratio rose in a flat consumption year, so EC is taking share, not riding the cycle — while the growth rate has normalised, from +9.23% in 2023 to +5.1% in 2024 on METI's B2C series. Yano names 3PL the largest domestic contributor to market growth in FY2024, FY2025 (forecast) and FY2026 (forecast): shippers are buying integrated services and supply-chain visibility, which is why 3PL grows at roughly twice the total market rate in Section 1.

The cold chain is the tightest physical market in the sector. Refrigerated warehouse volume under management reached 40.843m m³ at June 2025, up 6.3% year on year from 38.406m m³ [reported: MLIT Warehouse Statistics Quarterly, FY2025 Q1]. The Japan Refrigerated Warehouses Association reports 12-city warehouse-space occupancy of 94.4% (August 2026, 403 sites — an association measure, not a national vacancy rate), a shortage of about 5% in major metropolitan areas, industry profit margins of about 3%, and construction costs 30% to 40% above 2015. Most importantly for capex, 34% of refrigerated warehouses nationwide are over 40 years old, and 46% in Tokyo (January 2024). Replacement and natural-refrigerant conversion are a forced capex cycle, independent of demand growth — and demand itself is price-led: frozen-food consumption value rose 4.4% to a record ¥1,301.8bn in 2024 while consumption volume rose 1.5% [reported: Japan Frozen Foods Association]. A METI-basis food EC market size for 2024 was not obtained in this pass; the food-EC headroom argument is therefore qualitative here, and is labelled as such.

blocks.heading: Semiconductor and AIDC-related logistics — a qualitative tailwind only
blocks.html:
This report states the position plainly: no quantified series for Japan domestic warehousing demand attributable to semiconductors or AI data centres (AIDC) was obtained, and no number is invented for one. What exists in the sources is three kinds of evidence, none of which is a domestic warehouse-volume series. First, air freight: Yano (August 2026) expects air-freight demand for semiconductors, electronic components, pharmaceuticals and precision equipment to remain firm in FY2026, and Reuters (31 July 2026) reported Korean Air's second-quarter cargo revenue up 46% year on year on AI chips, server racks and data-centre infrastructure, with technology products accounting for about 80% of the increase in JAL's Asia-origin air exports (ex-China) over the past year. Second, equipment mix: cleanroom applications were 35.1% of JILS logistics-systems equipment sales in FY2024 [calculated share of the reported ¥657.0bn total]. Third, company strategy: Mitsubishi Logistics' Management Plan [2025–2030] names semiconductor and power-infrastructure-related logistics and healthcare cold chain among its category strategies.

The correct treatment is therefore qualitative: AIDC and semiconductor logistics are a high-value-density tailwind concentrated in air freight, precision handling and capacity near production clusters, supportive of the forwarding stage of the value chain in Section 3 and of names with air-freight exposure — it is not a quantified driver of domestic warehouse volumes in this report, and any initiation that capitalises it as one should be challenged on its source. The gap is recorded in Section 7.

blocks.heading: 3. Value chain — where the Big 3 sit, and where the margin sits
blocks.html:
Figure d1 sets out the chain: shippers and cargo owners; international forwarding; port transport and handling; warehousing and distribution processing (highlighted — the stage this sector is named for); land transport; and consignees and distribution. Underneath the chain sits a real-estate leg — leasing and asset recycling that monetise the land the chain operates on. The Big 3 occupy every stage: all three run warehousing, port operations, land transport and international forwarding, and all three own rental real estate. Mitsubishi Logistics is adding scale at the forwarding stage with the acquisition of all shares of Hankyu Hanshin Express for ¥120.11bn, announced on 30 October 2026 and expected to close in Q4 FY3/2027. MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS is the most 3PL-weighted of the three, built from acquired units in home-appliance logistics (2012), supply-chain solutions (2015) and land transport (2015). Sumitomo Warehouse integrates warehousing, port operations and international transport with a listed trucking subsidiary and overseas subsidiaries in the US, Europe, Singapore, Thailand and China.

The margin sits at the two ends of the chain that own scarce assets — property and customer integration — not in the physical middle. On reported FY3/2026 segment figures: Mitsubishi Logistics' real-estate segment earned a 33.0% operating margin against 5.3% for logistics; MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS' real estate earned 42.4% on its total including internal revenue (48.8% on external sales) against 8.4% for logistics; Sumitomo Warehouse's real estate earned 40.1% against 7.3% for logistics. In profit share the asymmetry is starker: real estate was 13.0% of Mitsubishi Logistics' external revenue but 47.9% of its segment operating profit, and 5.3% of Sumitomo Warehouse's revenue but 24.5% of its segment profit. Logistics real-estate market conditions set the terms on which the property leg can grow: Greater Tokyo large multi-tenant vacancy was 9.8% in Q4 2025 with effective rent of ¥4,490 per tsubo per month [reported: CBRE], Ichigo's broader Tokyo-area measure showed vacancy of 8.5% in October 2025, and both trackers forecast 2026 new supply below 2025 levels — CBRE at 524,000 tsubo for Greater Tokyo, below the 2016–25 average of 536,000 tsubo. This is a digestion phase, not a development boom: the 2023–24 completion wave is being absorbed, with the Ken-O-do submarket still at 15.0% vacancy in Q4 2025 against 4.0% at Tokyo Bay. A single citable national total for modern logistics facility stock was not obtained from the free CBRE or Ichigo releases, which publish flows and vacancy within their own surveyed universes.

blocks.heading: 4. The Big 3 — reported results and J-Core scenarios
blocks.html:
Figure 3 compares the Big 3 on reported FY3/2026 results. MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS is the largest by revenue at ¥299,472mn and the most profitable, with operating profit of ¥22,111mn and a 7.4% margin, helped by high-value air-freight demand — and it trades at the highest P/B, 1.73x at ¥3,199. Mitsubishi Logistics reported revenue of ¥273,446mn and operating profit of ¥15,928mn (5.8% margin); its FY3/2026 net income of ¥54,773mn includes a ¥67,281mn gain on sales of investment securities and is not a run-rate figure. Sumitomo Warehouse reported revenue of ¥196,244mn and operating profit of ¥11,413mn (5.8% margin) at a P/B of 0.93x at ¥3,835 — the only one of the three below book value — with net income supported by ¥5,132mn of Naniwa-suji line compensation and a ¥5,618mn gain on sales of policy shareholdings, neither of which is recurring operating earnings. All three companies also hold policy shareholdings that their plans commit to reduce — book values of ¥80.4bn (9301), ¥17.3bn (9302) and ¥201.3bn (9303) on EDINET DB data updated 24 November 2026 — a second, separable capital-release leg alongside real estate.

Figure 4 carries the scenario frameworks from the three initiation reports published today, 24 November 2026, which are the source for every target in this section [all J-Core estimates]: Mitsubishi Logistics, Overweight, base case ¥1,450 (+16.9%), bear ¥995 (−19.8%), bull ¥1,690 (+36.2%); MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS, Overweight, base case ¥3,800 (+18.8%), bear ¥2,560 (−20.0%), bull ¥4,300 (+34.4%); Sumitomo Warehouse, Overweight, base case ¥4,500 (+17.3%), bear ¥3,100 (−19.2%), bull ¥5,400 (+40.8%). The sector pattern is the finding: base cases cluster tightly at +17% to +19%, while the bear-to-bull ranges are 54.4 to 60.0 percentage points wide. A sector growing at +2% to +4% a year in yen does not produce 55-point outcome ranges by itself; the ranges are wide because the variables that decide them — rate pass-through delivery, automation-led margin, real-estate value surfacing through recycling and sales, and policy-share disposal — are management execution variables that differ by company. That is why this report rates the companies and not the sector.

blocks.heading: 5. The 29-company universe — Wave 1 today, Wave 2 in market-cap order
blocks.html:
The programme universe is the TSE 33-sector code 5200 roster verified against the JPX listed-company file dated 31 October 2026: 31 companies, of which two are excluded on scope — Tokyo Kisen (9193), a tugboat and ferry operator whose tug business was 72.4% of FY3/2026 sales, and Hyoki Kaiun (9362), where shipping was 56.8% of FY3/2026 sales against 43.2% for port and warehouse operations. The remaining 29 companies are in Figure 5. Wave 1 is the Big 3, initiated today. Wave 2 follows in market-cap order (Nikkei, retrieved 24 November 2026; FISCO for 9368) and starts with Kamigumi (9364) at ¥519.6bn — the sector's largest company by market cap, ahead of Mitsubishi Logistics at ¥434.7bn, and Japan's largest port operator. Market caps are a single-source snapshot for ranking only and move daily.

Three Wave 2 flags matter for sequencing. First, sub-cluster economics differ: K.R.S. Corporation (9369) is a food cold-chain business in the Kewpie group; PHYZ Holdings (9325), Kantsu HD (9326) and e-LogiT (9327) are EC-linked 3PL and fulfilment names, with PHYZ carrying single-customer concentration and e-LogiT loss-making in FY3/2026 with a ¥273m impairment and a sharp FY3/2027 downgrade on 13 November 2026. Second, several names carry non-core segments that must be valued separately — Asagami's legacy printing business (9311), Rinko's hotel segment (9355), and Kimura Unity's mobility, IT and staffing segments alongside its Toyota-group contract logistics (9368). Third, disclosure thins quickly below the Prime-market names: 21 of the 31 roster companies are Standard-market and one is Growth-market, and Kamigumi's financials sit outside the Wave 1 data set assembled for this report — they are marked not obtained for initiation purposes here and are the first data task of Wave 2.

blocks.heading: 6. Risks
blocks.html:
Price pass-through limits. The sector's yen growth is a price story, and price stories end. Warehousing has no standard-freight benchmark, storage fees were broadly flat from 2000 while construction costs rose, and Sumitomo Warehouse has already disclosed one plan miss caused partly by delayed pass-through. If shippers resist the next round of revisions — the JILS cost ratio already eased from 5.44% to 5.32% in the 2025 survey — yen revenue growth converges toward physical volume growth of 0% to 2%, and the mid-single-digit framing of this report fails.

Wage inflation and labour supply. Warehouse wage settlements reached 5.69% in FY2024 and the sector faces a projected shortfall of about 55,100 workers in FY2028. Operators that cannot convert scarcity into automation-led margin absorb the wage line directly; MLIT's FY2024 indicators already show cargo-handling divisions at a −3.3% average operating margin. Freight cyclicality compounds this: FY2024's +5.7% market growth included Red Sea ocean rates and yen weakness that Yano expects partly to reverse, and MITSUI-SOKO HOLDINGS' operating profit has already swung from about ¥26.0bn in FY3/2022–23 to ¥17.8bn in FY3/2025 and back to ¥22.1bn in FY3/2026 on the freight cycle.

Real-estate concentration and earnings cliffs. The asset leg cuts both ways: Greater Tokyo vacancy is still 9.8% on CBRE's measure, unrealised gains are pre-tax and appraisal-based, and realising them depends on transaction markets. At the majors, reported net income carries cliffs when one-off gains annualise out — Mitsubishi Logistics' FY3/2026 net income of ¥54,773mn contains ¥67,281mn of securities-sale gains, Sumitomo Warehouse's contains compensation and share-sale gains, and both companies' forward net income depends in part on planned policy-share sales (about ¥100bn of proceeds inside Mitsubishi Logistics' FY2025–30 cash plan; ¥60bn of sales in Sumitomo Warehouse's 2026–30 plan). Policy-share sales are finite: when the portfolios are sold down, the earnings line they supported goes with them. Finally, disclosure risk at small caps: most Wave 2 names are Standard-market companies with thin segment disclosure, single-customer or single-port concentration, and — in e-LogiT's case — demonstrated financial fragility. Position-level work on Wave 2 names requires the primary filings, not this sector summary.

blocks.heading: 7. Basis of preparation and source register
blocks.html:
Basis. This report was prepared on 24 November 2026 from the J-Core sector growth data pack of the same date, the programme universe document (UNIVERSE.md, roster verified against the JPX listed-company file dated 31 October 2026), and the Big 3 financial bases compiled from each company's FY3/2026 filings. Reported figures are as disclosed; forecasts are labelled with their owner throughout; calculated figures are arithmetic on a source's own published endpoints and are labelled as such. Share prices are the 24 November 2026 closes used in the three company initiation reports (9301 ¥1,240.5; 9302 ¥3,199; 9303 ¥3,835). Scenario targets are J-Core estimates from those reports, published 24 November 2026, cited here — they are not company guidance. The sector rating is Not Rated; company ratings sit in the company reports.

Earlier drafts of the growth pack also recorded the Big 3 rental real-estate book-versus-fair-value table as not obtained; that gap was closed from the FY3/2026 filings in the company data files, and the reported unrealised gains used in this report are ¥298,359mn (9301), ¥102,140mn (9302) and ¥88,048mn (9303). No figure in this report is interpolated or invented.
